# Surface Furrowing Instability in Everting Soft Solids

Jonghyun Hwang, Mariana Altomare, and Howard A. Stone∗

Department of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Princeton University, NJ 08544, USA (Dated: January 3, 2025)

We report a surface instability observed during the extrusion of extremely soft elastic solids in confined geometries. Due to their unique rheological properties, these soft solids can migrate through narrow gaps by continuously everting the bulk material. The extrusion front spontaneously buckles in the direction transverse to the flow, resulting in a furrow-like morphology that deepens over time. We characterize the distinct features of this instability using experiments and theory and contrast the results with known elastic surface instabilities. Our study may provide insights into various processes involving the extrusion-like deformations of soft solids, including biomaterials.

Soft materials exhibit various morphological features by virtue of their ready deformability. Often, mechanical interactions in soft materials cause surface buckling instabilities, which manifest periodic wrinkles, localized creases, or folds [1, 2]. These instabilities can be of significant interest for applications in engineering, such as controlled optical properties [3, 4] or predicting buckling modes of thin films [5], and also pose challenging theoretical questions. Surface instabilities have been studied primarily in the context of compression-driven instabilities, which arise from processes such as biological growth [6, 7], swelling [8, 9], or friction [10, 11]. Studies on elastic surface instabilities typically have involved soft solids whose shear moduli were O(103) Pa or larger. Recently, the mechanics of solids in an extremely soft limit, whose equilibrium storage moduli G0 = O(0.1−10) Pa, have gained attention, owing to their natural connection to soft, solid-like systems found in biology [12–14]. Because of the loosely connected network structure, these solids exhibit rate-, time-, and strain-dependent elasticity; similar rheological characteristics are found in imperfectly networked elastomers [15, 16]. Consequently, understanding the mechanical traits of these synthetic and biological ultrasoft solids is essential. This Letter presents a surface instability observed during the movement of ultrasoft solids within confinement; we are not aware of previous reports of the phenomenon documented here. We demonstrate that these solids can translocate through narrow gaps by continuously inverting their own body inside-out. This deformation process leads to the emergence of furrow-like surface grooves, forming primarily due to the solid gel’s ‘inside-out’ deformation, and distinct from previously known types of surface instabilities. We confirm this distinction theoretically and experimentally and offer a scaling analysis to explain the cause of the ‘furrowing’ instability. In our experiments, two acrylic cylinders, one hollow and the other solid, machined and surface-polished, were brought together to create a hollow annular channel of different widths d = 2w; the centerline radius of the hollow annular channel is denoted Rc [Fig. 1(a)]. The outer radius of the annulus

was Ro = Rc + w = [7.9, 12.6, 15.5, 21.9, 48] ± 0.3 mm, and we adjusted the radius of the inner cylinder to give eleven different values of w = [0.40, 0.65, 0.90, 1.15, 1.40, 1.65, 1.90, 3.10, 3.60, 4.55, 14.5]± 0.08 mm. Axisymmetric geometries were explored primarily due to having continuous boundaries to consider, whereas channels with rectangular cross-section introduce additional boundaries and corner effects; future experiments with long and narrow rectangular geometries may provide new insights. The viscoelastic gel material was cast and left to crosslink in the ‘reservoir’ below the annulus [Fig. 1(a)]. The viscoelastic gel was composed of vinyl-terminated polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) (viscosity µ = 4850 mPa·s; Gelest) and silicone oil (µ = 20.8 mPa·s; Sigma Aldrich). We first discuss the onset characteristics of the instability. The critical length ℓc was measured at varying crosslinker concentration c, strain rate ˙ε, the half-gap w, and the outer radius Ro [Fig. 2]. ℓc did not vary between different combinations of c and ˙ε, however, it was most strongly affected by the geometrical length scale w. Within the range of w studied, ℓc ∝w4/3. We explored the role of the confinement geometry more extensively and identified that ℓc ∝R−1/3 c ; thus we could organize all the data as ℓc ∼w4/3R−1/3 c [Fig. 2(a)] (see [20], § III).

While the surface morphology of the instability shown in Fig. 1 resembles those observed in the compressiondriven crease instability, we elucidate several key differences that set the instability documented here apart from the crease instability. The surface crease instability appears when a soft solid is compressed laterally greater than εcrease = 35.4 % of its initial length [25], or more if the effect of surface tension, γ, is significant. Localized creases are naturally aperiodic, but when the two length scales, the gel thickness, w, and the elastocapillary length, γ/G0, are comparable, periodically buckled surface pattern can form [26]. In such cases, the wavelength and the critical compressive strain depends on both w and γ/G0 [27]. The critical length for the instability increased to the prediction of the crease instability, which we confirm by performing a linear perturbation analysis (see [20], § IV). To explore the deformation of the solid gel within confinement, we mixed density-matched polystyrene beads (ρ = 0.96 g/cm3, 106-125 µm-diameter; Cospheric), and then tracked the position of the particles [Fig. 3(a)]. Once the surface was deformed, beads positioned underneath the furrowing folds stalled. As the gel progressed further into the annulus, some furrows grew, increasing λ. During this process, beads approaching the dead-end turned away and flowed into surviving, larger protuberances. The material trajectory of the elastic elements inside the curved tip region is similar to that of the fountain flow in viscous liquids, characterized by rotating toroidal vortices [Fig. 3(b)]. We call this type of solid deformation ‘eversion’. This observation evinces that soft solids can move in confinement by constantly turning their body inside-out. We note that the instability begins and propagates from the inner boundary, not at the apex of the extrusion front [Fig. 3(c)]. Also, the propagation of the instability happens much faster than the time scale of the extrusion ( ˙ε−1). This finite-time propagation is attributable to the gel viscoelasticity [25]. The everting path lines of the elastic gel element suggest that the instability observed here is shear-bendingdriven, rather than compression-driven. This leads to the conclusion that the instability differs from the crease instability and represents a phenomenon that has not been explored before, at least to our knowledge. Henceforth, we refer to the instability studied in this work as the ‘furrowing’ instability, drawing inspiration from its morphological resemblance to surface undulations that progressively deepen over time. In conclusion, our study demonstrates the remarkable deformability of soft solids, showcasing their ability to flow into narrow gaps by continuously everting their bodies through shear interaction with the confining walls. Prolonged eversion of the thin annular soft body resulted in a novel form of surface instability, we termed the ‘furrowing’ instability. Our experiments showed that the critical strain and the instability wavelength depend only on the geometric length scales. These findings shed light on fundamental aspects of material behavior and also carry implications for both industrial processes and biological systems, offering insights into the motion and stability of soft bodies within confinement.

## I. MICROSTRUCTURE AND RHEOLOGY OF VISCOELASTIC SOLIDS

We performed small amplitude shear oscillatory (SAOS) measurements to probe microstructural characteristics of our gel material. We used an Anton Parr MCR302e rheometer with a parallel plate geometry. The gel was cured overnight (≥15 hours) on the rheometer plate at room temperature. The diameter of the plate was 50 mm, and the gap between the plates was maintained at 1 mm. We used sandblasted surfaces to prevent slippage of the material on the surface. The frequency sweep measurement was performed at a constant 1% shear amplitude, from f = 0.001 Hz to 100 Hz. From this measurement, we obtained the frequency dependent complex modulus G∗(f) = G′+iG′′ [Fig. S1(a)].

Theory of the loosely crosslinked network - Measurement suggested the existence of an overarching network that encloses the sol elements (silicone oil) at crosslinker concentration c > 0.4 wt%. In this state, the material is rubber-like, and G′ > G′′ in the low frequency

limit. This rubber-like viscoelastic elastomer shows complex nonlinear relaxation phenomena, which can be modeled by considering relaxation process of dangling chains (side chains), such that Gk(t) ∼σk(t)P(k) [1], where k is the length of a dangling chain, σk(t) is the stress that is assumed to grow proportional to the un-relaxed length of the side chain, σk(t) ∝k−r(t) and P(k) is the probability of finding a side chain of length k. The relaxed portion of chain r(t) increases logarithmically in time [2]. Assuming mean field percolation, P(k) = q(1 −q)k−1, where q is the crosslink density normalized by the chain segment density. Summing the contribution to the stress over all possible chain lengths, one obtains,

G(t) = G0[1 + (τ/t)n] (S1)

where the exponent n is linearly proportional to q, and τ ∝(aq2)−b/q, where a and b are material parameters. Dynamic response of the viscoelastic solids can be found by computing the transfer function of the above expression [3], which gives,

G(s) = G0[1 + Γ(1 −n)(sτ)n] (S2)

where Γ is the gamma function and s is the transform variable s = 2πif, where i = √−1. Frequently, a simplified form of dynamic modulus that omits the gamma function from the above expression is used, and yet provides adequate fit [4]. Chasset and Thirion, who first empirically proposed this power-law relaxation function, noted the inadequacy of this expression to explain the long-time relaxation behavior (towards decreasing f, see Fig. S1(a,ii)) [5]. From this expression, storage and loss moduli can be obtained be seeking the real and the imaginary part of G(s), respectively.

Stress and strain response of the viscoelastic solid gel - Next, we performed amplitude sweeps to determine strain-dependent behavior of the material. In Fig. S1(b), we show the amplitude sweep result for a c = 0.45 wt % gel probed at varying shear oscillatory frequencies. We observe that at frequencies less than the crossover frequency, f < fc ≈0.1 Hz, strain stiffening is observed until the shear strain reaches the fracture strain εf ≈2500 %. For f > fc, strain stiffening follows initial softening of G′. This initial softening suggests straininduced relaxation of the side chains. Lastly, we measured the change in strain at a constant applied stress for c = 0.45 wt % gels. The time scale of the extrusion (inverse of strain rate ˙ε) ranges from 1 to 50 seconds. This is the time scale that a material element

Drawing a conclusion from this observation, we expect that the gel would recover almost its entire strain once the stress of O(G0) is removed after having been applied for 1 −50 seconds. Therefore, we consider that the material behavior is elastic for the timescales that we performed our experiments. Comment on viscous dissipation - We argue that viscous effects are negligible. Based on the observations made in Fig. 3(b) in the main text, we observe that material flows vertically upward near the central region of the gap and flows vertically downward following the relative motion of the confining walls. Therefore, upward-flowing and downward-flowing material interact – these two regions are not directly crosslinked with each other; therefore, interactions mainly come from dangling chains and the Newtonian solvents. We justify this assumption based on the composition of the material – a loose elastic network filled with low viscosity silicone oil. The timescale of the viscous interaction τviscous = η/G0 = O(10−2 Pa · s)/O(10−1 −10 Pa) = O(10−3 s) for stiff gels to = O(10−1 s) for soft gels. On the other hand, the time scale of the relaxation of the dangling chains τelastic, which we define as the inverse of the G′

and G′′ crossover frequency, is O(10−1 s) for stiff gels to = O(103 s) for soft gels. Also, the time scale of the extrusion τextrusion, which we define as the inverse of the shear rate, is O(100 s) to O(102 s). Therefore, τviscous ≪τelastic ∼τextrusion. Hence, we treat that elastic interaction as most relevant for the time scale of our experiment. Independence of ℓc and λ on c or G0 - In Fig. 2. of the main text, we show that ℓc and λ are independent of how cross-linked the gel is (thus c and G0) and of how fast the gel is being extruded into the annulus ( ˙ε). The explanation to the latter observation is physically intuitive as the response of the gel to the imposed stress, although being viscoelastic due to having dangling chains, is most strongly governed by the elasticity of the “infinite network” [6]. We still note that, once the extrusion is stopped, the buckled free surface slowly relaxes in amplitude to some extent (due to the time-dependent relaxation of the dangling chains) but maintains the overall shape. Although we did not quantify this observation, the time-scale of relaxation was qualitatively consistent with the relaxation time measured from the rheological

measurement. Next, the observation made with regards to the independence of ℓc on G0 was consistent in the range of G0 we explored in this study (G0 = 0.2 ∼55 Pa). Below c = 0.425 wt%, the material stayed below the gel point (thus having no “infinite network”) and there was no furrowing instability in the range of ˙ε we explored in this study. And above c = 0.55 wt%, the gel was too stiff to be extruded into the channel. We concluded that the key factor to observe the furrowing instability is the existence of the infinite network with high fraction of loose dangling chains.

## II. PERIODICITY OF THE FURROWING INSTABILITY

We performed image analysis on the snapshots of the side view videos to comment on the periodicity/aperiodicity of the surface instability. We used a Nikon D3300 with a 200 mm focal length lens; the camera imaged a segment of 12.1 - 16.1 mm. The ratio between the length of the segment (c) to the actual arclength (a) of the material in the curved geometry was 1:1.03 - 1.05. By using MATLAB Fast Fourier Transform feature, the periodicity of the initial wavelength was analyzed, and the method is described in Fig. S2. In the example shown in Fig. S2(a-d), the strongest frequency signal occurs at 0.83 mm-1. This suggests the number of the feature to be 0.83 mm-1 × 12.1 mm = 10, which agrees with our visual observation of n ≈10. From Fig. S2(e) through (h), we show four other examples with varied w/Rc.

## III. FURROWING INSTABILITY IN OTHER GEOMETRIES

In the main text, we presented experiments performed with annular geometries with the gel reservoir (see Fig. 1(a) in the main text). In this note, we present a couple of model experiments where we observe the furrowing instability in other geometries. In Fig. S3(a-c), we present experiments performed with hollow cylinders of various radii. In Fig. S3(d-e), we demonstrate the formation of the furrowing instability without the gel reservoir. In both experiments, there is no change in the nominal area (normal to the axial direction) in which the gel is confined during the extrusion of the gel. To analyze the data, we treat the hollow cylinder geometry as an annulus with its inner radius vtending to zero, Ri = Rc−w →0. Since w is defined as half of the gap between the two confining walls, w is then the radius of the hollow cylinder. Thus, we obtain ℓc ∼w4/3R−1/3 c ∼w [Fig. S3(a)]. Therefore, we hypothesize that the free surface of the gel confined inside a hollow cylinder would become unstable once extruded for ℓc ∼w, as discussed in the main text. An example is shown in Fig. S3(b). We performed experiments using c = 0.45 wt% gel extruded

The two sets of measurements have differences of a factor of 2, which we believes stems from the geometry changing from an annulus to a confined cylindrical channel, as illustrated in Fig. S3(a). Next, we describe the ‘without reservoir’ experiment. In our earlier experiments (described in Fig. 1(a) of the main text), we conducted tests using a setup comprising the ‘annulus’ and ‘reservoir’ sections. Gels entering the annulus from the reservoir may experience radial and circumferential compression. To ascertain that this compression is not the cause of the furrowing instability observed, we designed the ‘without reservoir’ experiment. We prepared an annulus of outer diameter 31 mm and inner diameter 25 mm. Then, we cast a c = 0.45 wt% gel in the gap of the annulus. The gel was cast on top of a ring-shaped plunger and left to cure overnight. Once the gel was fully cured, we pushed the annular cell casing the gel straight downward at a constant strain rate of ˙ε = 0.1 s−1, as illustrated in Fig. S4. Therefore, the ring-shaped plunger travels upward relative to the motion of the casing. The gel interface was initially flat; however, after some length ℓ, the free surface of the gel deformed and showed the furrowing instability. From the ‘hollow cylinder’ experiments and the annulus ‘without reservoir’ experiment, we conclude that the furrowing instability is not caused by the solid body compression, but rather appears whenever ‘eversion’ of the solid body occurs.

## IV. COMPARISON TO COMPRESSION-DRIVEN WRINKLING/CREASE INSTABILITY

Justification for a linear stability analysis - There is geometric similarity between the phenomenon considered in this article and the so-called ‘creasing’ instability [7, 8]. The creasing instability is a subcritical bifurcation of the Biot instability, which is the formation of localized surface wrinkles in a laterally compressed elastic block. Since creases form at a lower critical compressive strain compared to wrinkles, observation of the Biot instability had been a challenge. However, works of Mora et. al. [9] and Liu et al. [10] showed that in presence of strong surface interactions (increasing γ/G0L, where L is the characteristic length scale of the problem), the critical compressive strains of the two types of surface instability become alike. The work of Cao and Hutchinson characterize the creases as the ‘collapsed’ state of the wrinkle [11]. This suggests that one can perform linear

stability analysis to identify the critical condition for the formation of the surface instability, when the material experiences a strong surface effect. In this section, we will delineate the effect of squeeze compression on the formation of the surface instability by following the work of Cai et. al. [12] and Liu et. al [10].

Modeling solid body deformation - We start by describing the elastic deformation of a squeezed gel body, as described in Fig. S4. In Fig. S4(a, b), we show a set of schematics that describe the deformation of the gel in the ‘with reservoir’ case. The gel is compressed in the vertical direction, and then the gel elements squeezed outside R > Ri further deform to fit inside the annulus. Thus, we decompose the deformation in two steps. Typically, the total deformation gradient is obtained by multiplying the deformation gradients in different steps. However, since we assume inhomogeneous deformation for the second step in the deformation, we set the total deformation gradient to be the composition of the independent deformations, F = F2(F1). Because the gel is incompressible, the radial and azimuthal components of the deformation gradient are chosen to satisfy det(F1) = 1. Assuming a homogeneous axisymmetric deformation, i.e., the deformation is the same throughout the sample, the first step in the deformation can be described with F1 = diag(φ−1/2, φ−1/2, φ), where φ is the final length divided by the initial length, hence a measure of stretch. This changes the height of the gel to be ∆h = (φ −1)H. Through this deformation, material is squeezed and moves homogeneously from the center radially outward. Next, the second step in the deformation F2 describes how the excess portion of the squeezed material (r > Ri) would deform to fit within the annular section. During the second step of deformation, the inner boundary of the annulus is prescribed such that the squeezed material in r < Ri does not deform. We will write F2 with a set of arbitrary stretches, F2 = diag(χr, χθ, χz) and express each component as a function of geometry and the squeeze compression φ. In the case that the annular curvature κ = w/Rc is small, one can assume the deformation in the radial direction is homogeneous. With this assumption, the material in [(Rc −w), φ−1/2(R + w)] will be homogeneously deformed to [(Rc −w), (R + w)] [Fig.S4(a)]. The radial compression associated with this deformation is then

χr = 2κ/[φ−1/2(1 + κ) −(1 −κ)]. (S3)

Next, azimuthal compression is the change in the radius of the centerline component of the gel before and after the deformation. Specifically, the centerline radius of the squeezed portion of the gel (in the intermediate state [see the middle panel in Fig. S4]]) is Rc,int = Ri+(φ−1/2R0− Ri)/2. This line element is deformed to Rc = Ri + w in the current state. Then, the corresponding compression ratio in the azimuthal direction is

χθ = Rc/Rc,int = 2/[φ−1/2(1 + κ) + (1 −κ)]. (S4)

We stress again that the model is valid in the limit where w is small compared to Rc. This experimental observation confirms that furrowing instability is a distinct mode of surface instability from the crease instability.

## VII. EXPERIMENTAL METHODS

Syringe fabrication – We fabricated cylindrical annulus at varying gaps using off-the-shelf cast acrylics. Extruded acrylics were not suitable for our experiment because the extruded materials typically have rough extrusion lines on the surface of the material. We lathed the cast acrylic rod (for example, McMaster Carr item No. 8528K53) down to varying diameters to fabricate the inner cylinder in the annulus. These machined parts were polished with 1000 grade sand paper with water, and ultrasoft jewelry polishing cloth. The outer, hollow cylinder part of the annulus was fabricated from McMaster Carr, for example, item No. 8486K331. We 3D-printed the syringe plunger (Form 2 printer, FormLabs) and used an O-ring of appropriate size to seal the gap between the 3D printed parts and the machined hollow cylinders.

Before the extrusion – We cast the gel in the gel reservoir (see Fig. S8) and let it cure for overnight (approximately 15 hours). The height of the cast gel is kept approximately the same as the diameter (2Ro) of the channel. Also, the distance between the start of the annular section to the free surface of the cast gel was about 1.5 ∼2Ro. We kept this ratio throughout the experiments for consistency, but changing this initial distance may provide new insights. This distance must not be larger than 2Ro as the gel can develop furrowing instability just by flowing inside a hollow cylinder (ℓc ≈2.7Ro; see Fig. 2(a) in the main text).

During the extrusion – Once the gel is fully cured, the gel was pushed vertically upward with a syringe pump (PHD Ultra, Harvard Apparatus) at varying flow rates as input to the pump. Given a field of view of our lens, the side view video filmed the region of an arclength of 12 mm to 16 mm. Because the feature size of our interest was typically ˜1 mm or less in its size, we could take average of the 10 to 20 furrows in each experiment. For the side view, we used Nikon D3300 with a lens with

200mm focal length. For the top view, we used Nikon D5100 with an 18-55mm lens. After each experiment, the acrylic parts were disassembled and were thoroughly cleaned with ethanol to remove PDMS residue. The furrowing instability begins from the inner boundary (Ri) and propagates outward to (Ro). We defined ℓc as the position of the apex of the free surface when the apex starts to furrow downward, instead of when the inner contact line starts to furrow. This is because the camera is positioned outside (looking into the annulus from the side) and the view is distorted if one would try to observe the inner contact line through the curved surface. Also, as the propagation of the instability is much faster than the time scale of the extrusion (see Fig. 3(c) in the main text), this brief lag of time for the instability to propagate from Ri to the apex did not affect our result. Likewise, the furrow depth a was measured from when the apex starts to furrow downward.

# GUIDE: Guided Updates for In-context Decision Evolution in LLM-Driven Spacecraft Operations Accepted at CVPR 2026 AI4Space Workshop

**Authors:** Alejandro Carrasco Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, USA Email: acarra@mit.edu Mariko Storey-Matsutani Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, USA Email: m_storey@mit.edu Victor Rodriguez-Fernandez Affiliation: Universidad Politecnica de Madrid Affiliation: Madrid, Spain Email: victor.rfernandez@upm.es Richard Linares Affiliation: Massachusetts Institute of Technology Affiliation: Cambridge, USA Email: linaresr@mit.edu

## Abstract

Large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as supervisory agents for spacecraft operations, but existing approaches rely on static prompting and do not improve across repeated executions. We introduce GUIDE, a non-parametric policy improvement framework that enables cross-episode adaptation without weight updates by evolving a structured, state-conditioned playbook of natural-language decision rules. A lightweight acting model performs real-time control, while offline reflection updates the playbook from prior trajectories. Evaluated on an adversarial orbital interception task in the Kerbal Space Program Differential Games environment, GUIDE’s evolution consistently outperforms static baselines. Results indicate that context evolution in LLM agents functions as policy search over structured decision rules in real-time closed-loop spacecraft interaction.

## 1 Introduction

Spacecraft operations remain costly, high-risk, and slow to iterate. Unlike most terrestrial AI deployments, missions cannot easily collect large amounts of new data, reset the environment, or retrain policies after deployment. Yet many operational scenarios—exploration missions, autonomous Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC), on-orbit servicing, and non-cooperative interaction—require supervisory reasoning under uncertainty rather than only low-level control. This creates a gap between existing autonomy algorithms and operator-level decision making, motivating systems capable of reasoning under uncertainty and adaptability rather than relying on fixed policies.

Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising candidates for this supervisory layer [12, 2]. Beyond text generation, they exhibit reasoning, hierarchical agentic behavior, and structured decision making [15]. Modern LLM systems can also alter behavior at inference time through in-context learning and memory without updating weights, making them attractive where retraining is impractical and deployment constraints dominate.

Deploying an LLM as a supervisory decision agent in a real-time, closed-loop dynamical system introduces two coupled constraints. First, control actions must be generated within strict latency bounds while reasoning over delayed feedback, irreversible actuation, and adversarial interactions. Models capable of extended deliberation incur prohibitive latency for direct integration into the control loop, whereas models that meet real-time requirements cannot perform such reasoning during action selection. Second, interaction with reactive or unknown agents requires adaptation across encounters rather than one-shot decisions. Because such adaptation cannot occur inside the online loop, learning must be separated from action execution. This dual constraint motivates a teacher–student separation, in which a frontier reasoning model performs episodic offline reflection while a lightweight acting model executes real-time control.

Building on the paradigm of large language models as spacecraft operators [12, 3, 2], we introduce GUIDE (Guided Updates for In-context Decision Evolution), a non-parametric policy improvement framework that enables cross-episode adaptation without parameter updates. Instead of optimizing parameters, the system iteratively refines a state-conditioned playbook—a structured set of natural language rules encoding contextual behavior guidance—which functions as a non-parametric policy representation. The acting model remains fixed; policy improvement arises from updating this context rather than model weights, enabling adaptation to adversarial dynamics while preserving real-time execution. We show that structured in-context memory can serve as a learnable policy object improved across episodes without parameter updates.

To study this setting, we consider a real-time multi-agent Capture-the-Satellite scenario using the Kerbal Space Program Differential Games (KSPDG) environment [1]. The environment involves sequential decision-making under delayed observations and non-cooperative interactions, providing a closed-loop setting in which cross-episode adaptation can be evaluated under realistic dynamical constraints.

## 2 Related Work

Spacecraft autonomy requires sequential decision-making under delayed observations and irreversible dynamics, particularly in adversarial and non-cooperative scenarios [6, 10]. While classical GNC provides reliable stabilization and trajectory tracking when objectives and models are specified [3], it does not address strategic objective selection. This motivates a supervisory decision layer above conventional control, for which recent work has explored LLMs as operator-like decision modules for spacecraft tasks [12, 3, 2].

More broadly, LLM-agent research studies systems combining reasoning, memory, and tool use within action loops [14, 15], but these agents accumulate errors and exhibit prompt sensitivity in long-horizon tasks [14]. A key observation is that behavior can adapt at inference time through in-context learning (ICL): instead of weight updates, the model conditions on demonstrations and memory to modify its decisions [4, 5, 8]. This has been interpreted as inference-time meta-learning [4], and reflection mechanisms incorporate experience without gradient-based retraining [13, 9, 11].

Agentic Context Engineering (ACE) treats structured context as the persistent object of improvement across executions [16], with related self-evolving systems refining structured experience across runs [17, 7]. Our framework is closest in spirit to ACE but differs in objective and role: rather than using evolving context solely to guide behavior, the context itself becomes the learned decision representation that shapes the actions of an online agent. Unlike prior self-evolving agents, which are typically evaluated in episodic software environments, we study context evolution within a continuous closed-loop dynamical control system.

## 3 Method

*Figure 1: Closed-loop control with cross-episode context adaptation. A fixed acting model executes $\pi(a\mid s,P_{k})$ online, while offline reflection updates the playbook via add/update/remove and UCB selects improved versions.*

We propose GUIDE, a framework for language-based decision agents in real-time closed-loop tasks (Fig. 1). The key idea is to learn state-conditioned behavioral guidance expressed in natural language (a playbook) and iteratively improve it using episodic reflection over executed trajectories. Instead of updating model parameters, the method performs a search over structured rules, while a resource-constrained language model executes actions online.

### 3.1 Problem Setting

We consider sequential decision problems defined over continuous spacecraft dynamics. At each timestep $t$ , the agent observes state $s_{t}$ and produces a control action $a_{t}$ . State transitions are governed by orbital mechanics, and thrust actions irreversibly influence future trajectories.

Experiments use the KSPDG environment, which simulates adversarial orbital encounters under varying initial conditions and maneuver policies. We evaluate the Lady–Bandit–Guard (LBG) interception scenario, where the agent controls the bandit spacecraft $B$ , attempting to minimize its distance to the lady spacecraft $L$ while avoiding capture by the guard spacecraft $G$ . At each timestep, the agent observes elapsed time $t$ , spacecraft mass ( $m_{prop},m_{total}$ ), and CBCI-frame position and velocity vectors for all relevant spacecraft, yielding

$$ s_{t,LBG}=\{t_{LBG},m_{B,total},m_{B,prop},\vec{B},\dot{\vec{B}},\vec{L},\dot{\vec{L}},\vec{G},\dot{\vec{G}}\}, $$

where $\vec{B},\dot{\vec{B}}$ denotes the bandit’s position and velocity, $\vec{L},\dot{\vec{L}}$ the lady’s, and $\vec{G},\dot{\vec{G}}$ the guard’s. The control action $a_{t}$ is a three-axis thrust vector with an associated burn duration [1].

Guard behavior varies across scenarios. In LG4, the Guard follows an aggressive pursuit policy, directly chasing the Bandit. In LG6 and LG7, the Guard adopts a defensive strategy, remaining near the Lady and positioning along likely interception trajectories. LG5 introduces stochastic switching between pursuit and defense. These regimes are not specified in prompts or observations and are not known a priori to the LLM policy generator.

### 3.2 Playbook Representation

Rather than learning a policy $\pi_{\theta}(a|s)$ through gradient optimization, action selection is conditioned on a language-structured context $\pi(a|s,P)$ , where $P$ is a dynamic playbook providing state-conditioned behavioral guidance.

The acting model receives a fixed baseline prompt encoding generic domain instructions (e.g., guard avoidance and prograde alignment for interception). This baseline remains constant across all experiments and is not modified during training.

The playbook $P$ is initially empty and evolves over episodes. It is represented as a collection of bullets or natural language rules, optionally annotated with a state predicate $b_{i}=(\text{text}_{i},\text{condition}_{i}(s))$ , where a bullet becomes active when its condition evaluates to true (e.g., distance thresholds or approach conditions). Active bullets are injected into the prompt at runtime, augmenting the fixed baseline context and modifying the decision distribution.

The learned object in our framework is therefore not the model parameters nor the fixed baseline prompt, but the evolving playbook $P$ .

### 3.3 Online Decision Agent

The acting language model executes control decisions at every timestep using the playbook-conditioned policy $\pi(a\mid s,P)$ . To ensure real-time compliance while preserving structured reasoning, the model is decomposed into two sequential calls within each control cycle.

First, a bounded reasoning agent (fixed token budget) produces short-horizon intent conditioned on the current observation and the active playbook bullets. All strategic decision-making occurs within this reasoning step, and the playbook $P$ directly shapes the model’s deliberation through state-conditioned behavioral rules injected into context.

Second, an actor agent maps the state and the generated intent to a structured control output via a function call tool. This stage produces no free-form reasoning and is restricted to the control action format required by the environment.

This separation bounds reasoning latency while allowing the evolving playbook to shape strategic behavior; the actor simply enforces structured execution within the control interface.

### 3.4 Offline $\epsilon$ -Biased Reflection Sampling

After batches of episodes, trajectories are evaluated by the meta-reasoning LLM using task performance metrics and constraint violations. Reflection inputs are not chosen solely from failures. Instead, an $\epsilon$ -selection rule is used: with probability $1-\epsilon$ , the system reflects on poorly performing trajectories, and with probability $\epsilon$ , it reflects on successful ones. Each reflection input consists of a short telemetry window together with the reasoning trace that produced the corresponding decisions.

A frontier language model (Reflector) analyzes the selected episode and proposes behavioral corrections. A second pass (Curator) converts these proposals into structured operations applied to a rule-based playbook, producing new rules for a new playbook version $P_{k}$ :

$$ \{\text{ADD},\text{UPDATE},\text{REMOVE}\}, $$

Multiple playbook versions are maintained simultaneously and evaluated over complete episodes. Selection among playbooks uses an Upper Confidence Bound (UCB1) rule

$$ \text{score}_{k}+c\sqrt{\frac{\log N}{n_{k}}}, $$

where $n_{k}$ is the number of evaluations of version $k$ and $N$ is the total number of evaluations. This favors playbooks that perform well while still allowing newly generated versions to be tried.

The acting model performs real-time control using the current playbook, while the frontier model operates only between episode batches to revise the playbook from accumulated trajectories. The two models, therefore, serve complementary roles: online execution and offline policy improvement.

## 5 Conclusions & Future Work

GUIDE demonstrates that LLMs can adapt online to dynamic adversarial scenarios through structured context evolution, without weight updates. Beyond static spacecraft operation, context evolution enables cross-episode policy improvement under unpredictable agent interactions, which is most impactful when baseline policies are far from optimal.

Future work includes ablation studies, tighter low-level control integration, algorithmic candidate evolution alongside language policies, and larger-scale playbook evolution to assess convergence behavior.

# Spacecraft Rendezvous Trajectory Generation with Modular Constraints via Diffusion Model Composition

**Authors:** Mariko A. Storey-Matsutani ††thanks: Graduate Student, Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Massachusetts Inst. of Technology, Cambridge MA Richard Linares ††thanks: Associate Professor, Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics, Massachusetts Inst. of Technology, Cambridge MA

## Abstract

Emerging mission classes such as on-orbit servicing, satellite inspection, and active debris removal require trajectory design methods that are adaptable to a variety of mission scenarios. We present a diffusion-based trajectory generation approach for rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) that enables flexible configuration of mission constraints. First, individual energy-based diffusion models are trained to satisfy distinct constraints such as approach cone and sensor line-of-sight from a set of optimized trajectories. Then, at inference time, the learned energy models can be composed with one another, or with an analytically defined energy field, to enforce specific constraint combinations. We validate this framework with the composition of a learned approach cone model and a learned sensor line-of-sight model, as well as a learned approach cone model and synthetic obstacle avoidance model, both of which yield constraint satisfaction rates that are within 1 percentage point of the single-constraint models or higher. These results indicate that our compositional diffusion framework can provide a modular approach to RPO trajectory design and enable reconfiguration for new constraint combinations without requiring model retraining.

## 1 Introduction

In recent years, rapidly growing interest in space-based infrastructure has accelerated the need for advanced trajectory design methods. In particular, emerging mission classes such as on-orbit servicing, active debris removal, and in-space assembly have emphasized a focus on rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) maneuvers, which require spacecraft to operate in close proximity while satisfying dynamical and safety constraints [29]. The ongoing NASA Artemis program and commercial space station development efforts further motivate the need for robust autonomous RPO capabilities to expand human presence in space, as tasks like docking and resupply are prime examples of critical RPO maneuvers [26].

The relative motion dynamics for RPO regimes are commonly modeled using linearized formulations such as the Clohessy–Wiltshire (CW) or Hill equations [29, 5]. However, practical missions require further optimization methods to yield fuel-optimal trajectories that are typically prioritized in space missions [22]. Despite the benefit of these linearized models, trajectory design for RPO is fundamentally challenging because the close coordination of spacecraft introduces tightly coupled constraints that require full, six degree-of-freedom motion planning. The consideration of approach cone, sensor line-of-sight (LOS), plume impingement avoidance, and collision avoidance constraints can introduce nonconvex feasible regions in the state-control space [29].

As shown in classical optimal control literature, one approach to solving such nonconvex trajectory optimization problems is sequential convex programming (SCP), which has been applied to RPO mission applications.[20] SCP works by iteratively approximating a convex subproblem of the original nonconvex problem formulation, which enables the application of traditional convex optimization methods [21, 30]. While SCP has demonstrated strong performance in many path planning scenarios, its convergence can be sensitive to initialization and the addition or modification of constraint sets requires reformulation of the convexification strategy. [15] As missions increasingly rely on coordinated, multi-spacecraft operations in cislunar and Earth-orbit environments, there is a need for modular, flexible tools for trajectory design that can adapt to changing mission needs.

Given these limitations, recent work has explored learning-based alternatives for the generation of spacecraft trajectories. Reinforcement learning [4], imitation learning [25], and transformer-based architectures [2, 10, 31, 13] have been used to approximate optimal policies or directly generate feasible trajectories, as well as to warm-start traditional solvers for nonconvex optimal spacecraft control. However, many existing approaches exhibit limited generalization across varying constraint configurations. As a result, changes in constraint geometry or combinations typically necessitate retraining, thus reducing flexibility and limiting deployment in adaptive mission contexts [3, 17].

To this end, existing research has begun to explore the application of diffusion models as an alternative approach to generative trajectory design [3, 23, 17]. Diffusion probabilistic models are a type of generative model capable of representing complex multimodal distributions through an iterative denoising process [12, 28]. Originally developed for high-dimensional data such as images[12], diffusion models learn probabilistic distributions over solution spaces and allow conditioning mechanisms that are well-suited for trajectory generation problems [14]. In particular, the formulation of diffusion models as energy-based models further supports model composition and posterior conditional sampling, enabling constraint-flexible trajectory generation without model retraining [7].

Diffusion-based models have recently been applied to several spacecraft trajectory problems, including powered descent guidance, low-thrust transfers, and ballistic transfer generation [3, 1, 9, 23]. These works show that diffusion models can learn complex solution manifolds, provide diverse and high-quality initial guesses, and accelerate warm-starting of indirect and direct optimal control solvers [3, 17, 9]. However, most existing applications focus on single-vehicle scenarios with relatively structured constraints, and do not directly address RPO-specific constraints like approach cones, collision avoidance, and sensor line of sight.

This gap motivates the compositional diffusion framework for RPO trajectory generation developed in this work. Instead of training a single complex model to satisfy all mission constraints simultaneously, we demonstrate the decomposition of the constraint space into modular components and train individual diffusion models on distinct constraint classes (e.g. approach cone, sensor line-of-sight). At inference time, these models are composed to generate trajectories that satisfy multiple constraints concurrently, enabling reconfiguration to new RPO mission constraint profiles while reducing retraining requirements.

## 2 Methodology

We propose a two-phase framework for generating warm-start trajectories for rendezvous and proximity operations (RPO) under modular constraint profiles. In the first phase, individual diffusion models are trained on constraint-specific expert trajectories that are generated offline using sequential convex programming (SCP) via the SCPToolbox framework [19]. In the second phase, these diffusion models are composed and conditioned at inference time to generate trajectories that satisfy flexible constraint combinations. The following sections detail the key elements of this framework, including data generation, diffusion model training, and composition operations.

### 2.1 SCP-Based Data Generation

Expert trajectories are generated using the Apollo CSM rendezvous example provided in SCPToolbox. [19] The relative translational dynamics between the two spacecraft are modeled using the linearized Clohessy–Wiltshire (CW) equations in the local orbital frame, while the rotational motion is represented through rigid-body attitude dynamics under thruster actuation [19]. The trajectory’s initial state is randomized within a defined range to generate diverse rendezvous scenarios.

The system state and control vectors are defined as

$$ x_{k}=\begin{bmatrix}r_{k}\\
v_{k}\\
q_{k}\\
\omega_{k}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{13},\qquad u_{k}=\begin{bmatrix}f_{k}\\
f_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}}\\
f_{k}^{\mathrm{eq}}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{33}. $$

Here $r_{k}$ and $v_{k}$ denote the relative position and velocity in the local orbital frame, $q_{k}$ represents the spacecraft attitude quaternion using scalar-last convention, and $\omega_{k}$ denotes the angular velocity. The control vector contains the commanded thruster forces $f_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{16}$ , the reference thruster forces $f_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}}\in\mathbb{R}^{16}$ , and a scalar slack variable $f_{k}^{\mathrm{eq}}\in\mathbb{R}$ used to enforce the minimum-impulse firing logic [19]. Expert trajectories are generated by solving the following trajectory optimization problem based on the Apollo CSM rendezvous scenario implemented in SCPToolbox [19]:

$$ \begin{array}[]{r l}\displaystyle\min_{\{x_{k},u_{k}\}_{k=0}^{N-1},t_{f},\Delta x_{f}}&\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}w_{k}\left(\frac{\mathbf{1}^{\top}f_{k}}{f_{\max}}+\gamma_{c}\frac{f_{k}^{\mathrm{eq}}}{f_{\min}}\right)\\
&\text{s.t.}\\
\text{Dynamics:}&x_{k+1}=f_{d}(x_{k},u_{k},t_{f}),\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-2\\
\text{Initial state:}&x_{0}=x_{\mathrm{init}}\\
\text{Docking condition:}&x_{N-1}+\Delta x_{f}=x_{\mathrm{dock}}\\
\text{Terminal position tolerance:}&\|\Delta r_{f}\|_{\infty}\leq r_{\mathrm{tol}},\qquad\xi^{\top}\Delta r_{f}=0\\
\text{Terminal velocity tolerance:}&\|\Delta v_{f}\|_{\infty}\leq v_{\mathrm{tol}}\\
\text{Terminal angular rate tolerance:}&\|\Delta\omega_{f}\|_{\infty}\leq\omega_{\mathrm{tol}}\\
\text{Attitude alignment:}&q_{N-1}^{\top}q_{f}\geq\cos\!\left(\frac{\theta_{\mathrm{tol}}}{2}\right)\\
\text{Thruster limits:}&0\leq f_{k,i}\leq f_{\max},\qquad\forall i=1,\ldots,16\\
\text{Reference thrust limits:}&0\leq f_{k,i}^{\mathrm{ref}}\leq f_{\max},\qquad\forall i=1,\ldots,16\\
\text{Control allocation slack:}&\|f_{k}-f_{k}^{\mathrm{ref}}\|_{1}\leq f_{k}^{\mathrm{eq}},\qquad k=0,\ldots,N-1\\
\text{Final time bounds:}&t_{f}^{\min}\leq t_{f}\leq t_{f}^{\max}\\
\text{Minimum thruster firing constraint:}&f_{k,i}-\mathrm{OR}_{\kappa}\!\left(f_{k,i}^{\mathrm{ref}}-f_{\min}\right)f_{k,i}^{\mathrm{ref}}\leq 0\\
\text{Reference thrust consistency:}&\mathrm{OR}_{\kappa}\!\left(f_{k,i}^{\mathrm{ref}}-f_{\min}\right)f_{k,i}^{\mathrm{ref}}-f_{k,i}\leq 0\\
\text{Additional path constraints:}&s(x_{k},u_{k};\kappa)\leq 0\end{array} $$

We focus on defining the distinct constraints that were used to demonstrate the compositional nature of the proposed diffusion-based trajectory generation framework: the approach cone constraint and the sensor line-of-sight (LOS) constraint. Separate datasets are generated for each constraint, with a common set of base RPO constraints (dynamics, docking, thruster, and minimum-impulse logic) and the distinct additional path constraint $s(\cdot)$ .

The approach cone constraint restricts the vehicle to approach the target from a specified direction once within a distance threshold $r_{A}$ :

$$ \cos\theta_{A}-\frac{r_{k}^{\top}\xi}{\|r_{k}\|}\leq 0,\qquad\text{when }\,\|r_{k}\|<r_{A}. $$

This constraint ensures that the spacecraft’s relative position $r_{k}$ lies within a cone of half-angle $\theta_{A}$ aligned with the docking axis $\xi$ when the vehicle enters the terminal approach region of radius $r_{A}$ . The distance-dependent activation is implemented through $\mathrm{OR}_{\kappa}$ , a homotopy-parameterized approximation to the logical disjunction that enforces the angular restriction once the spacecraft is within the approach distance threshold [19].

The sensor line-of-sight constraint seeks to maintain the chaser’s target visibility over the full trajectory. This requires the body-fixed sensor axis to remain pointed toward the target within a sensor viewing angle, as defined by

$$ \cos\theta_{S}-b\cdot\hat{r}\leq 0. $$

This constraint enforces that the angle between the chaser’s body-fixed sensor axis $b$ and the target direction $\hat{r}$ remains below a threshold $\theta_{S}$ throughout the trajectory.

The resulting trajectories are filtered for numerical validity and dynamic feasibility. To reduce the dimensionality of model training, the $16$ commanded RCS thruster forces are aggregated into a net three-axis force and torque vector, yielding a 6-dimensional control representation. Combined with the 13-dimensional spacecraft state, this yields a 19-dimensional feature vector discretized over 50 time steps. This feature vector is normalized per-feature to have zero mean and unit standard deviation ( $\mu=0,\sigma=1$ ) prior to training. The parameters for the generated data are given in Table 1.

### 2.2 Diffusion-Based Trajectory Modeling

Diffusion model training involves a forward “noising” process that gradually corrupts the input data as a neural network learns the reverse “denoising” process to reconstruct the input. While standard diffusion models apply independently sampled Gaussian noise to each state, this assumption neglects the strong temporal dependencies inherent in trajectory data. To address this limitation, we adopt the Dynamical Diffusion formulation introduced by Guo et al. [11], which incorporates an explicit temporal coupling mechanism into the forward process.

Given a trajectory $x_{0}=\{x_{0}^{s}\}_{s=0}^{S-1}$ , the forward process constructs noisy samples by combining Gaussian diffusion with a recursive dynamics operator. At diffusion step $t$ , the corrupted trajectory is defined as

$$ x_{t}^{s}=\sqrt{\bar{\gamma}_{t}}\left(\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,x_{s}^{0}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\epsilon_{t}^{s}\right)+\sqrt{1-\bar{\gamma}_{t}}\,x_{t}^{s-1},\qquad\epsilon_{t}^{s}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I), $$

where $\bar{\alpha}_{t}$ is the cumulative diffusion noise schedule and $\bar{\gamma}_{t}$ governs the strength of temporal coupling between adjacent trajectory states. As $\bar{\gamma}_{t}$ increases, the process places greater emphasis on local state information, while smaller values promote stronger temporal smoothing [11].

This construction can be equivalently expressed through a dynamics transformation operator $\Phi(\cdot,\bar{\gamma}_{t})$ applied recursively along the trajectory:

$$ x^{\mathrm{dyn}}=\Phi(x,\bar{\gamma}_{t}),\qquad x^{s,\mathrm{dyn}}=\sqrt{1-\bar{\gamma}_{t}}\,x^{s-1,\mathrm{dyn}}+\sqrt{\bar{\gamma}_{t}}\,x^{s}, $$

with initialization $x^{0,\mathrm{dyn}}=x^{0}$ . The same operator is applied to both the clean trajectory and the Gaussian noise, yielding $x_{0}^{\mathrm{dyn}}=\Phi(x_{0},\bar{\gamma}_{t})$ and $\epsilon_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}}=\Phi(\epsilon_{t},\bar{\gamma}_{t})$ . This ensures that both signal and noise share consistent temporal structure [11].

We adopt an energy-based formulation of diffusion models [7], in which the model learns a scalar energy function $E_{\theta}(x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}},t)$ over the dynamics-transformed trajectory. The model is trained via standard denoising score matching, such that the scaled energy gradient approximates the temporally-conditioned noise via

$$ \mathcal{L}(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_{x_{0},t,\epsilon_{t}}\left[\left\|\epsilon_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\nabla_{x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}}}E_{\theta}(x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}},t)\right\|^{2}\right]. $$

During sampling, we reverse the diffusion process iteratively from Gaussian noise. At each step $t$ , the current sample is transformed via $x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}}=\Phi(x_{t},\bar{\gamma}_{t})$ , and a noise estimate is obtained from the energy gradient:

$$ \hat{\epsilon}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{dyn}}(x_{t},t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}\nabla_{x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}}}E_{\theta}(x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}},t). $$

This is mapped back to untransformed coordinates via the inverse dynamics operator:

$$ \hat{\epsilon}=\Phi^{-1}(\hat{\epsilon}_{\theta}^{\mathrm{dyn}},\bar{\gamma}_{t}),\quad\text{where}\quad x^{s}=\frac{x^{s,\mathrm{dyn}}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\gamma}_{t}}\,x^{s-1,\mathrm{dyn}}}{\sqrt{\bar{\gamma}_{t}}}. $$

The clean trajectory prediction is then given by

$$ \hat{x}_{0}=\frac{x_{t}-\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t}}\,\hat{\epsilon}}{\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t}}}, $$

which is fed into a standard reverse diffusion update to obtain $x_{t-1}$ . To accelerate sampling, we employ a DDIM (Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models) sampler [27], which uses deterministic reverse steps instead of the stochastic updates of DDPM (Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models) [12]. This enables fast sampling with 50-100 denoising steps while maintaining comparable sample quality.

The energy network $E_{\theta}$ is realized with a U-Net architecture, a standard choice for diffusion models due to its ability to capture multi-scale feature interactions [12, 6, 24]. Trajectories are encoded as single-channel $50\times 19$ tensors (50 time steps, 19 features) and processed through a symmetric encoder–decoder with convolutional blocks, layer normalization, and swish activations. Skip connections between matching encoder and decoder levels preserve fine temporal detail. The diffusion timestep $t$ is encoded via sinusoidal embeddings and additively injected into each block to condition the network on the noise level. The final convolutional layer produces a feature map that is spatially summed to yield the scalar energy $E_{\theta}(x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}},t)$ . The input gradient of this energy function ( $\nabla_{x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}}}E_{\theta}$ ) serves as the score estimate used during training and sampling. ### 2.3 Constraint Composition and Conditioning

The energy-based formulation enables inference-time composition of independently trained models without retraining [7]. In particular, multiple constraint models can be combined by manipulating their probability densities or corresponding energy functions during sampling. Two composition operators are considered in this work: product composition, which enforces simultaneous satisfaction of multiple constraints; and negation composition, which suppresses trajectory regions associated with undesirable constraint energies. Following Briden et al. [1, 3], we define product and negation composition as weighted sums of learned energy functions applied during DDIM sampling. Let $p_{i}(x)$ denote the trajectory distribution learned for constraint set $i$ , with corresponding energy function $E_{i}(x)$ . These operators are defined as

$$ \text{Product:}\quad E_{\mathrm{prod}}(x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}},t)=\sum_{i=1}^{K}w_{i}E_{i}(x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}},t),\qquad w_{i}>0 $$

$$ \text{Negation:}\quad E_{\mathrm{neg}}(x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}},t)=\alpha E_{1}(x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}},t)-\beta E_{2}(x_{t}^{\mathrm{dyn}},t),\qquad\alpha,\beta>0 $$

where $K$ is the number of component models, $w_{i}$ are nonnegative composition weights, and $\alpha,\beta$ control the relative influence of attractive and repulsive energy terms [7, 8, 1, 3].

In addition to the composition of learned energy models, we investigate the composition of a learned energy model with an analytically-defined energy field, which offers a simpler approach for constraints with predictable energy landscapes. For example, to encourage obstacle-avoidance behavior at inference time, we artificially generate an energy field whose values are highly negative at the obstacle location and decay in magnitude with radial distance. The synthetic obstacle energy is defined as

$$ E_{\mathrm{obs}}(x)=g\sum_{t}\left[-\operatorname{softplus}\left(-\frac{\|p_{\mathrm{phys}}(t)-c\|_{2}-(R-\sigma)}{\sigma}\right)\right], $$

where $p_{\mathrm{phys}}(t)$ is the position of the spacecraft at time $t$ in physical units, $c$ is the obstacle center, $R$ is the obstacle radius, $\sigma$ is the softening length, and $g$ is the gain. All other dimensions besides position are given an energy value of zero. This synthetic energy field is then composed with a learned energy model via negation composition to yield a composed model that respects both the obstacle avoidance and learned model constraints.

Aside from full model composition, inference-time conditioning can be applied through trajectory inpainting. During the iterative denoising process, inpainting fixes selected feature values to prescribed targets at each step while the remaining features are updated by the learned reverse process. At each reverse step, the clean-trajectory estimate $\hat{x}_{0}$ is computed as above; the entries in the inpaint set $\mathcal{M}$ are overwritten with their target values, and the modified estimate is used in the subsequent reverse diffusion update, as in Equation 13. By repeatedly re-imposing the fixed values throughout sampling, the diffusion process generates trajectories that remain consistent with the specified constraints [32, 16]. We employ this inpainting mechanism to condition the final position of the trajectory to the docking site, while allowing the remaining portions of the trajectory to be generated by the diffusion model. The general inpainting formulation is

$$ x_{t-1}^{s}=\sqrt{\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\;\tilde{x}_{0}^{s}+\sqrt{1-\bar{\alpha}_{t-1}}\;\hat{\epsilon}^{s},\qquad\tilde{x}_{0}^{s}=\begin{cases}y^{s}&\text{if }s\in\mathcal{M}\ \text{(inpaint region)}\\[3.99994pt]
\hat{x}_{0}^{s}&\text{if }s\notin\mathcal{M}\ \text{(non-inpaint region)}\end{cases} $$

where $\mathcal{M}$ indexes the fixed inpaint region (e.g. the position at the final trajectory timestep) and $y^{s}$ is the overwriting trajectory data (e.g. the target position) [18].

Together, these operations enable flexible inference-time manipulation of learned trajectory distributions, allowing constraint composition and partial trajectory conditioning without retraining the underlying diffusion models.

## 3 Results

This section evaluates the compositional diffusion-based framework for RPO trajectory generation. Our objective is to determine whether energy-based model composition and synthetic energy shaping can enforce combined constraints at inference time without any additional training. In addition to constraint satisfaction, the models are evaluated on their ability to learn or preserve feasible trajectory dynamics and fuel optimality. Unless otherwise noted, all diffusion trajectories are generated with 50 DDIM steps and metrics are computed over 100 generated samples per model with a 50-step discretization per trajectory sample.

### 3.1 Individual Model Performance

We first characterize each single-constraint model in isolation to establish that neither trivially satisfies the other’s constraint, thereby motivating a meaningful composition study. One model is trained on the approach cone constraint of Equation 3 and one on the sensor line-of-sight (LOS) constraint of Equation 4.

*Figure 1: 3D plot of Approach Cone-Only and LOS-Only Trajectory Samples*

The 100 samples drawn from each model are shown in Figure 1, and per-constraint metrics are reported in Table 3 along with training data metrics for reference. The satisfaction metric measures the mean fraction of constraint-active timesteps satisfying the constraint, while the peak violation metric measures the mean (across samples) of the maximum angular constraint violation along each trajectory’s constraint-active region. Each model closely satisfies the constraint on which it was trained, while exhibiting significant violations for the other. The approach cone model holds the approach cone over $96.1\%$ of constraint-active timesteps, while its sensor pointing is effectively unconstrained. The approach cone model satisfies the LOS constraint at only $24.2\%$ of constraint-active timesteps and exhibits a mean peak violation of $104.8^{\circ}$ . Conversely, the LOS model satisfies the LOS constraint at $99.6\%$ of constraint-active timesteps but satisfies the approach cone at only $36.9\%$ of constraint-active timesteps with a mean peak violation of $20.2^{\circ}$ . This confirms a compelling scenario for composition, since the two constraints are non-trivial and neither single model satisfies both constraints.

In addition to constraint satisfaction, we investigate the dynamic feasibility of the generated samples. Since the denoising process of diffusion sampling simultaneously generates the full trajectory output, it is necessary to validate that the generated state and control values are self-consistent. By re-propagating each sequence of diffusion-generated controls through the 6-DOF dynamics and measuring the resulting position error, we obtain a mean position error of $7.19\pm 3.45\,\mathrm{m}$ for the approach cone model and $5.88\pm 3.64\,\mathrm{m}$ for the LOS model. Although this dynamic consistency can improve with further model training, the discrepancy motivates the use of diffusion-generated trajectories as warm starts to traditional solvers, which can restore dynamic feasibility. While diffusion models can produce trajectories that are comparable to the SCP solutions, they offer no formal guarantee of dynamic feasibility or optimality. Instead, the diffusion model output can be used to warm-start a traditional optimal solver like the SCP solver used to generate the training data, such that the SCP solver can recover a dynamically feasible and locally optimal solution.

Figure 2 presents the mean propagated position error and total control effort across each propagation approach, where control effort accounts for both translational and rotational actuation. We find that the combination of diffusion-warm-started SCP and subsequent controls regeneration via position-based inverse dynamics yields the best balance between error and control minimization. In Figure 3, we provide a comparison of solve time, fuel optimality, and constraint satisfaction across cold-started SCP, warm-started SCP, and diffusion-only approaches. Over a sweep of $100$ seeds per model with $10$ denoising steps, the warm start combined with position-based inverse dynamics controls reduces the mean end-to-end solve time by $28.3\%$ for the LOS model and $29.4\%$ for the approach cone model. Furthermore, with both the cold-start and warm-start approaches, the constraint satisfaction rate remains consistent. The cold-start SCP process achieves a constraint satisfaction of $100.0\%$ for the LOS constraint and $95.9\%$ for the approach cone constraint, while the warm-start approach achieves $100.0\%$ for the LOS constraint and $96.8\%$ for the approach cone constraint. Furthermore, these time improvements are accompanied by less than a 3.5% increase in SCP-converged control effort for the LOS model and $0.4\%$ for the approach cone model.

The pure diffusion samples were generated with 50 DDIM steps and the performance metrics are provided as a point of comparison. While the sampling speed is much faster and the constraint satisfaction is comparable, the pure diffusion approach does not guarantee optimality or dynamic consistency. On the other hand, the warm-started SCP and position-based inverse dynamics approach achieves comparable fuel consumption and constraint satisfaction, and converges nearly 30% faster compared to the cold-started SCP approach.

### 3.2 Joint Constraint Satisfaction

The product-composed model was obtained according to the following energy composition:

$$ E_{\mathrm{prod}}(x)=0.1\,E_{LOS,\;6\text{-}DOF}(x)+0.9\,E_{appch,\;3\text{-}DOF}(x), $$

where $E_{LOS,\;6\text{-}DOF}(x)$ denotes the sensor line-of-sight energy model and $E_{appch,\;3\text{-}DOF}(x)$ denotes the translational subspace of the 6-DOF approach cone energy model. The weights were selected based on a parameter sweep analysis and act on the shared translational dimensions while the rotational dimensions are defined solely by the LOS model. We validate empirically that the rotational policy learned by the LOS model generalizes to the approach cone-constrained trajectories. ## 4 Discussion

This framework couples diffusion-based generative modeling with inference-time energy composition to produce constraint-modular RPO trajectories. The presented results support three claims.

First, diffusion models can generate constraint-satisfying RPO trajectories that reduce end-to-end solution time when used to warm-start a traditional SCP solver. The diffusion-warm-started solve with position-based inverse dynamics reduces end-to-end wall-clock time by roughly $30\%$ (including the cost of generating the diffusion sample) at a control-effort penalty of $\leq 3.5\%$ and with constraint satisfaction preserved. Notably, this speed-up stems less from a reduction in SCP iterations than from better-conditioned convex subproblems. The constraint-aware initial guess places the SCP solver closer to the feasible manifold and thus lowers the per-iteration cost. Furthermore, the near-identical converged fuel cost confirms that the warm start trades little to no optimality for speed. In short, the diffusion sample supplies a constraint-aware, near-optimal initial guess that can be paired with a traditional solver to certify dynamic feasibility and local fuel optimality.

Second, composition can induce combined constraint behavior without retraining and with minimal constraint penalty. Product composition yields a model that satisfies the approach cone and sensor-LOS constraints at $99.3\%$ and $98.6\%$ of constraint-active timesteps respectively, despite each single-constraint model satisfying the competing constraint at only $24$ – $37\%$ . Relative to each constraint-specific model, the product modestly exceeds the approach cone constraint satisfaction by 3.2 percentage points, while incurring a slight reduction of 1.0 percentage points in the satisfaction of the LOS constraint.

Third, learned energy landscapes can be composed with synthetic energies to extend the framework beyond pre-trained models. Across $100$ samples, the negation-composed model achieves $100\%$ satisfaction of the obstacle-avoidance constraint while preserving the base approach cone satisfaction at $96.5\%$ of constraint-active timesteps. Because the obstacle term is analytic, new keep-out constraints can be specified and enforced at sampling time without obstacle-specific training data or retraining, which can be an advantageous capability for mission scenarios that demand quick adaptation to unseen obstacle configurations. However, an introduced synthetic energy can degrade trajectory smoothness depending on the barrier form and composition parameters, motivating well-tuned barriers or use as a warm start.

Several limitations qualify these findings. First, the analyses are empirical, drawn from $100$ samples on a single rendezvous scenario, and should be read as observations rather than guarantees. The warm-start approach remains the only component that certifies dynamic feasibility and local optimality. Additionally, the composition weights and energy parameters were manually tuned for this work, and a real deployment would require systematic calibration. In particular, when constraints act on different state subsets or bind over overlapping time windows, naive weighting can let some energy fields dominate and suppress joint satisfaction. Finally, dynamic consistency is enforced only weakly during generation and is not explicitly considered during composition. The product-composed samples exhibit larger re-propagation error than the single-constraint samples, and should therefore be validated through the warm-start optimizer.

Future work could include physics-informed training and composition to tighten dynamic feasibility and fuel optimality without the warm-start framework. Additionally, the synthetic energy approach can be expanded beyond obstacle avoidance, to constraints like keep-out and corridor constraints. Finally, further study of the composition method could explore principled weight calibration or additional composition operators for new constraint types.

## 5 Conclusion

In this paper, we present a diffusion-based RPO trajectory generation approach, in which independently trained, single-constraint energy-based models are composed at sampling time to enforce unseen constraint combinations without additional training. Three findings support this framework. First, the single-constraint models can reproduce intended constraint behavior with high fidelity. Second, product composition of the learned models can yield joint satisfaction of nontrivial constraints. Third, composing a learned energy with a closed-form energy field can extend the framework to unseen constraints.

Since diffusion samples carry no formal feasibility or optimality guarantee, we pair them with the same sequential convex programming solver used to generate the training data, warm-starting it to cut end-to-end wall-clock time by roughly $30\%$ with minimal control-effort penalty and with constraint satisfaction preserved, yielding a dynamically feasible, locally fuel-optimal maneuver. Inference-time composition thus provides a flexible, retraining-free mechanism for multi-constraint RPO trajectory generation, and the diffusion-warm-started SCP pipeline provides a practical route from constraint-aware samples to deployable trajectories. Broader initial-condition and geometry sweeps, systematic weight calibration, and dynamics-informed training and composition remain as future work.
